title: When the Undertow Falls
premise: Hazel Vane, a celebrated restaurant critic who lost the sense of taste years ago and has never told anyone, returns to their decaying coastal hometown when the childhood house—the one where their sister Dora drowned and where their father's quiet cruelties went unrecorded—goes up for auction. Sorting through the house, Hazel uncovers a box of Dora's belongings suggesting the drowning was witnessed, and that the town's beloved harbormaster, now a dying local patriarch, may have been responsible and protected ever since. As the auction clock ticks, Hazel must choose between the safety of silence and a public reckoning that could cost them their career, their few relationships, and their fragile grip on memory. In the end, Hazel speaks—at the auction, before the whole town—naming both Dora and their father's complicity, and walks out of the house for the last time able, for the first time in years, to taste salt on the air.
about_author: Silas Vane is the pen name of a former line cook turned essayist who spent a decade writing about food before admitting they could no longer taste it. They live near a cold coast and write, in their words, 'only about the things people swallow instead of saying.'

chapters.title: A Palate of Ash
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. In the city, Hazel files a glowing review of a meal they cannot taste, then eats plain bread alone to test—again—whether the sense has returned. A letter arrives: the Vane house on Merrow Point is entering probate auction. The beat is quiet dread masked as routine; Hazel's invisibility is shown as a discipline, not an accident.

chapters.title: Inventory of Unsaid Things
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Hazel catalogs the review copies, the unopened letters from their mother, the voicemail from their estranged brother Theo they've never answered. The auction date gives them thirty days. Emotional beat: the reader sees Hazel's meticulous silence as both armor and prison, and the first crack of obligation.

chapters.title: The House Remembers Differently
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Hazel arrives in the coastal town of Gullmere and walks the house before the estate agent comes. Rooms trigger sensory flashes—dinner table tension, Dora's laughter—while the sea outside is flat and indifferent. Beat: grief arrives as architecture; Hazel realizes they came to say goodbye but doesn't know to whom.

chapters.title: Theo, Who Stayed
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo, who never left Gullmere and runs the hardware store, learns Hazel is back from a customer's gossip. We see his resentment and his own buried knowledge of that summer. He decides not to seek Hazel out. Beat: two silences growing in parallel, each believing the other chose the silence first.

chapters.title: The Harbormaster's Chair
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. At the dockside diner, Hazel is recognized and warmly received by Edmond Pryce, the aging harbormaster, a town patriarch who once gave Hazel free crab rolls. His charm lands wrong now; Hazel notices how everyone defers to him. Beat: unease—the reader feels power's warmth and its cost before Hazel names it.

chapters.title: Dora's Box
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Clearing the attic, Hazel finds a shoebox: Dora's diary, a child's drawing of the boathouse with a figure in it, and a broken watch stopped at 4:17—the hour of the drowning. The diary trails off days before her death. Beat: the past stops being memory and becomes evidence; Hazel's hands shake for the first time.

chapters.title: What the Water Took
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV, intercut with fragments of the diary. Hazel reconstructs the official story—Dora slipped, their father drank, the town closed ranks—and finds the seams: why was Pryce's skiff out that afternoon? Beat: the investigation begins as compulsion, not decision; Hazel tastes nothing but cannot stop.

chapters.title: The Auction Notice
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo attends the pre-auction viewing, sees Hazel across the crowded parlor, and they exchange four flat sentences about plumbing. Theo knows something about that day he has never said—that he saw Pryce's boat. His silence is now a choice with a body in it. Beat: guilt sharpened by proximity.

chapters.title: A Review of Small Mercies
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Hazel's editor calls: the Pryce family wants Hazel to write a farewell profile of Edmond for the town's centennial supplement—good money, good optics before the auction. Saying yes means access; saying yes means complicity. Hazel says yes. Beat: the moral hinge, disguised as a professional favor.

chapters.title: Interview with a Kind Man
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Hazel interviews Pryce in his cluttered office over the harbor. He is generous, funny, and casually devastating—'Your father never could hold his tongue, and look where it got him.' Hazel asks, lightly, about the summer Dora died. Pryce's smile doesn't move. Beat: the predator revealed through courtesy, not menace.

chapters.title: Mother's Voicemail, Played Twice
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. In the house at night, Hazel finally plays the eleven-year-old voicemail from their mother, now in a care home: 'You were there, Hazel. You saw something. Come tell me before I forget how to listen.' Beat: Hazel's amnesia about that afternoon may be protective, chosen, or convenient—and they can no longer tell which.

chapters.title: The Care Home by the Sea
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Hazel visits their mother, Ruth, who drifts between lucidity and fog but fixes on one thing: 'Edmond rowed out that day. Your father knew. They buried it together, over a bottle.' Ruth begs Hazel to say it out loud, somewhere it counts. Beat: permission granted; terror begins.

chapters.title: Theo's Ledger
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Hazel confronts Theo at the hardware store. Theo admits he saw the skiff from the dunes, told their father, and was told to forget it—then did, for thirty years, building a life on the forgetting. He refuses to go public but gives Hazel the exact date and time. Beat: brothers break open; alliance without absolution.

chapters.title: The Centennial Committee
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Hazel drafts the Pryce profile, a masterpiece of double meaning, and reads it to the centennial committee. Pryce's son Marcus, the auction's driving bidder, praises it warmly—too warmly. Hazel realizes the family wants the profile as a shield before the auction closes the estate forever. Beat: Hazel sees the machinery of reputation at work.

chapters.title: Salt in the Throat
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. A small miracle: eating fried clams at the diner, Hazel tastes them—faintly, then fully. The return of taste coincides with the return of the repressed afternoon: Dora on the dock, Pryce's skiff circling, their father watching from the window and doing nothing. Beat: sensation and memory flood back together; Hazel weeps over clams.

chapters.title: Marcus Makes an Offer
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Marcus Pryce offers to buy Hazel's silence wrapped in generosity: a paid column, help securing the house before auction, 'a fresh start.' The price is killing the profile and letting the past stay past. Beat: the corruption of power offered gently; Hazel almost says yes, and hates the almost.

chapters.title: The Diary's Last Page
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Under a lamp with a magnifier, Hazel finds Dora's final diary entry, written in pencil and smudged: 'E.P. said if I tell, the crabs will know. He was angry about the nets. I'm going to tell anyway.' Beat: the evidence is a child's sentence—fragile, undeniable, devastating. Hazel stops being a witness and becomes a voice.

chapters.title: What Silence Costs
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo, unable to live with it, tells his wife everything; she says, 'Say it where they can hear you or stop punishing yourself.' Theo decides to stand with Hazel after all. Beat: Theo's arc turns—from keeper of the secret to its second witness. The siblings reconcile over the hardware store's closing bell.

chapters.title: The Night Before the Auction
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Hazel files the Pryce profile as written—truthful, unflinching, naming the nets dispute and the skiff—knowing it will run the morning of the centennial, hours before the auction. Pryce calls: 'You'll be finished in this town.' Hazel answers, 'I was never in it.' Beat: the point of no return, calm and terrified.

chapters.title: The Reading of the Profile
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. At the centennial gathering, the profile is read aloud as planned. Murmurs, then uproar. Pryce, frail in the front row, demands Hazel retract; instead Hazel stands and says Dora's name, and the diary line, and their father's silence, out loud, before everyone. Beat: climax—justice spoken outside any courtroom, at personal ruin.

chapters.title: Going, Going
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. The auction proceeds amid scandal; Marcus withdraws rather than buy the house now attached to his father's name. A young couple from out of town wins it. Hazel walks the empty rooms once more, says goodbye to Dora properly—out loud, at last—and locks nothing. Beat: release; the house becomes someone else's memory.

chapters.title: The First Meal
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV, closing. Weeks later, Hazel's column runs under a new byline policy: no more meals they cannot taste. Hazel and Theo share crab rolls at the diner where Pryce's chair sits empty; the town is still deciding what to do with the truth. Hazel tastes everything—the brine, the butter, the grief. Final beat: justice incomplete but spoken; memory carried, not buried; Hazel stays visible.
